block.heading: Demand elasticity on a diagram
block.text:
Assume straight demand lines and unchanged other demand conditions. A shop sells 100 packets a week each of maize meal and one brand of crisps at N$20. Both prices rise 50 per cent, to N$30. Maize meal sales fall 25 per cent, to 75 packets: PED is −0.5, inelastic. Crisps sales fall 75 per cent, to 25 packets: PED is −1.5, elastic. Few close substitutes can make demand less elastic; competing brands can make it more elastic.

![Demand elasticity diagram](diagrams/item-6145-3.3-019-proc-answer.png)

From that point the flatter curve is more elastic over this change. With different scales or starting points, steepness alone does not show elasticity, which also varies along a straight demand line.

item.prompt: A shop sells 100 packets a week of maize meal and 100 packets a week of one brand of crisps, each at N$20 a packet. Both prices rise to N$30. Weekly sales of maize meal fall to 75 packets and sales of the crisps fall to 25 packets. Assume straight demand lines and unchanged other demand conditions. Use these data to draw both demand curves on the same axes, with price on the vertical axis. Show the change for each product and label each curve with its price elasticity of demand (PED), calculated from the initial values (4).
item.canonical_answer: Draw both demand curves through the original point R (100, N$20) on the same labelled axes: price (N$ per packet) vertically, quantity demanded (packets per week) horizontally. The maize meal curve also passes through (75, N$30) and the crisps curve through (25, N$30); an arrow along each curve shows the movement from R as price rises. Price rises by 50 per cent. Maize meal: −25% ÷ 50% = −0.5, so demand is inelastic (magnitude below 1). Crisps: −75% ÷ 50% = −1.5, so demand is elastic (magnitude above 1). Because both curves share the same axes and starting point, the flatter crisps curve is the more elastic one over this change.
